issues.legal_issue: A person without a proprietary interest may maintain a constitutional writ petition when authorized to represent an affected body or otherwise prejudicially affected by the challenged act.
material_facts: The petitioner represented a village committee that collected and deposited contributions toward establishing a public health centre.
His conduct and the committee members’ acquiescence supported the finding that he was authorized to act for the committee, which held the collected amounts for a public purpose.
The challenged decision prejudiced the petitioner and the committee’s interests.
issues.conclusion: The petitioner had standing to maintain the petition under Article 226.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 ordinarily requires the petitioner to assert a personal or individual legal right, but that right need not be proprietary and may arise from a trustee’s interest. In exceptional cases, a person prejudicially affected by an authority’s act may petition even without a proprietary or fiduciary interest. The Court relied on The Calcutta Gas Company (Proprietary) Ltd. v. The State of West Bengal.

predicates.constitutional_writ_petition: A person files a petition seeking constitutional writ relief against an authority’s act.
predicates.authorized_representative: The petitioner is authorized to represent a body whose interests are affected by the challenged act.
predicates.personally_prejudicially_affected: The challenged act prejudicially affects the petitioner.

issues.definition: A constitutional writ petition is maintainable when the petitioner represents an affected body or is personally prejudicially affected.

issues.legal_issue: A subordinate rule cannot transfer to the government a statutory function vested in another body by making that body merely recommendatory.
material_facts: The statute vested the local governing body with the function of establishing and maintaining primary health centres.
The rules made that body merely recommendatory on the location of a centre and gave the government the final decision-making power.
The government relied on those rules to direct the location of the centre.
issues.conclusion: The rules were inconsistent with the statute and invalid to the extent that they deprived the local governing body of its statutory power and transferred that power to the government.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 18 and 69 of the Andhra Pradesh Panchayat Samithis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1959, read with the Schedule, the local governing body held the statutory function of establishing and maintaining primary health centres. The government’s rule-making power was limited to carrying out the purposes of the Act and could not transfer a statutory function vested in another body.

predicates.challenge_to_subordinate_rule: A party challenges a subordinate rule as inconsistent with the statute under which it was made.
predicates.statute_assigns_function_to_another_body: The statute assigns a function to a body other than the rule-making authority.
predicates.rule_makes_assigned_body_merely_recommen: The subordinate rule deprives that body of decision-making power and leaves it only a recommendatory role.

issues.definition: A subordinate rule is invalid to the extent that it makes a body merely recommendatory for a function assigned to it by statute.

issues.legal_issue: An order substantively cancelling a local body's resolution under a special statutory power cannot be reviewed under a general review power limited to orders made under that general power.
material_facts: The government’s earlier order rejected a local body’s resolution to locate a health centre elsewhere, reasoning that the resolution lacked the required support.
The order’s substance was to cancel that resolution, even though it did not use the word “cancel” or identify the specific statutory power.
The government later purported to review that order under the general review provision.
The special cancellation power required an opportunity for the local body to explain, while the general review provision permitted review only of an order made under its general revision power.
issues.conclusion: The earlier order was made under the special cancellation power and could not be reviewed under the general review provision; the government could not review it under the special power after becoming functus officio.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 62 and 72 of the Andhra Pradesh Panchayat Samithis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1959, distinguish the special power to cancel a local body’s resolution from the general revision and review powers. The principle generalia specialibus non derogant excludes matters governed by the special power from the general provision. Section 72(3) permits review only of an order made under section 72(1). The special power is quasi-judicial; after exercising it, the government is functus officio as to that order, and section 13 of the Madras General Clauses Act, 1891 does not authorize its review.

predicates.government_review_of_prior_order: The government purports to review an earlier order concerning a local body's resolution.
predicates.prior_order_substance_cancels_resolution: The earlier order rejects or nullifies a local body's resolution, whatever terminology the order uses.
predicates.special_cancellation_power_applies: A specific statutory power governs cancellation of the local body's resolution.

issues.definition: A government review of an order that substantively cancels a resolution under a special power is unavailable under a general review power.

issues.legal_issue: The government must give the local governing body an opportunity to explain before cancelling its resolution under the special statutory cancellation power.
material_facts: The government cancelled the local governing body’s resolution without giving that body an opportunity to explain.
The order was made under the special statutory power to cancel such a resolution.
issues.conclusion: The cancellation order was unlawful because the government failed to provide the required opportunity to the local governing body.
issues.legal_principle: Section 62(2) of the Andhra Pradesh Panchayat Samithis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1959, requires the government to give the local governing body an opportunity for explanation before acting under section 62(1); the requirement is mandatory.

predicates.special_cancellation_proceeding: The government considers cancelling a local governing body's resolution under a specific statutory cancellation power.
predicates.resolution_cancelled: The government cancels the local governing body's resolution.
predicates.governing_body_given_no_opportunity_to_e: The government does not give the local governing body an opportunity to explain before cancelling its resolution.

issues.definition: A cancellation order is unlawful when the government cancels a local body's resolution without first giving that body an opportunity to explain.

issues.legal_issue: A mistaken belief that a facility had been permanently located at a particular place is a factual mistake supporting review when the facility was never permanently located there.
material_facts: The earlier government order proceeded on the impression that the health centre had been permanently located at the original place.
The original place had not satisfied the conditions for permanent location before the relevant statutory body acted.
The statutory body later cancelled its earlier resolution in favour of that place and resolved to locate the centre elsewhere.
issues.conclusion: Assuming the earlier order was made under the general review provision, the government correctly found that it had been based on a mistake of fact.
issues.legal_principle: Section 72(3) of the Andhra Pradesh Panchayat Samithis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1959, permits review of an order made under section 72(1) when it was passed under a mistake of fact or law, or in ignorance of a material fact. The Court held that the belief in permanent location was mistaken because the necessary conditions had not been fulfilled and the later resolution favouring that location had been cancelled.

predicates.government_review_proceeding: The government considers reviewing an earlier order on the basis that it was made under a mistake.
predicates.prior_order_assumed_permanent_location: The earlier order proceeded on the belief that a facility had been permanently located at a particular place.
predicates.facility_was_not_permanently_located: The facility had not in fact been permanently located at that place.

issues.definition: A qualifying factual mistake exists when a government review concerns an earlier order founded on a belief in permanent location that was not true.

issues.legal_issue: A government review order that prejudicially affects a party is invalid if the party is not given an opportunity to make a representation.
material_facts: The government’s later order changed the location of the health centre and prejudicially affected the representatives of the village that had sought its location there.
The government made the order without giving the petitioner or the committee an opportunity to make a representation.
issues.conclusion: The later order was unlawful because the government failed to give the prejudicially affected representatives an opportunity to make a representation.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to section 72(1), applied to review proceedings by section 72(3) of the Andhra Pradesh Panchayat Samithis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1959, prohibits an order prejudicial to a party unless that party has had an opportunity to make a representation.

predicates.government_review_proceeding: The government conducts a review proceeding concerning an earlier order.
predicates.review_order_prejudices_party: The resulting review order prejudicially affects a party or its representative.
predicates.party_given_no_opportunity_to_make_repre: The affected party or representative is not given an opportunity to make a representation before the order is made.

issues.definition: A review order is unlawful when it prejudicially affects a party who was not given an opportunity to make a representation.

issues.legal_issue: A court may refuse discretionary writ relief where quashing an unlawful order would restore an earlier unlawful order and defeat a valid decision of the competent body.
material_facts: Both the government’s earlier cancellation order and its later review order were unlawful for different reasons.
The local governing body had validly resolved to locate the health centre at the alternative place.
Quashing the later order would have restored the earlier order and displaced the local governing body’s valid resolution.
issues.conclusion: The High Court properly refused to quash the later order in the exercise of its extraordinary discretionary jurisdiction, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 confers extraordinary discretionary jurisdiction. The Court may decline to grant relief where quashing the challenged order would revive an unlawful order and produce a result contrary to a valid resolution of the competent statutory body.

predicates.constitutional_writ_proceeding: A party seeks discretionary constitutional writ relief against an authority's order.
predicates.challenged_order_unlawful: The order challenged in the writ proceeding is unlawful.
predicates.quashing_would_restore_unlawful_prior_or: Quashing the challenged order would restore an earlier unlawful order.
predicates.valid_competent_body_decision_would_be_d: Restoring the earlier order would defeat a valid decision of the body legally empowered to decide the matter.

issues.definition: Discretionary writ relief may be denied when quashing an unlawful order would restore an unlawful prior order and defeat a valid decision of the competent body.
